abstract: Recent research by Liana Zanette and colleagues1 in Current Biology from South Africa's Kruger National Park heightens awareness of wildlife's perception of humans as a 'super-predator'. It reveals that a wide range of savanna animals flee and avoid humans significantly more than other predators when hearing auditory cues. This creates disquiet amongst biologists and protected area managers, as it poses the question of whether the activity of conservation work has itself a negative effect on wildlife. Other research corroborates this effect across numerous biomes2,3,4. Neutral or mutualistic relationships between humans and wildlife may induce tolerance or even attraction5, but where persecution or predation persist, the 'super-predator' label is emerging as a general rule. Protected areas should incorporate the outcomes of this research within their management frameworks. An ongoing attempt at this is described here.
